failing_part: "a t reference on the number of participants minus 2 degrees of freedom ... since each participant contributes one residual to the sandwich variance"
narrowest_regime: None as stated. The correct small-sample reference for a two-arm CRT analysed by GEE with a (bias-corrected) sandwich is t on K - 2 df, where K is the number of clusters.
reason: The sandwich 'meat' is a sum of K independent cluster-level score outer products, U_i U_i^T, so its rank and effective information are bounded by the number of clusters, not by the number of participants. Li & Redden (2015), the cited source, use and recommend K - 2 df (clusters minus the two cluster-level parameters) and warn that near-normal references should be avoided with few clusters. With N - 2 df the reference is essentially z: for K = 10 the critical value is about 1.97 where it should be 2.31 (t_8), so intervals come out roughly 15% too narrow and anti-conservative, which is exactly the failure Li & Redden document.

citations.cite: Li P, Redden DT. Small sample performance of bias-corrected sandwich estimators for cluster-randomized trials with binary outcomes. Stat Med 2015;34(2):281-296 (recommends Wald t with K - 2 df, K = clusters)

bite_note: With K < 40 clusters, t on N - 2 df is close to z, which narrows the intervals and inflates type I error. It changes whether the arm effect is reported as significant and how wide its interval is.

failing_part: "A feature whose D-ratio ... is 50% or less carries too little biological variance relative to technical variance and is removed"
narrowest_regime: The rule holds only with the inequality reversed: remove a feature whose D-ratio (SD_QC / SD_study x 100%) exceeds 50%, and keep those below it, preferably well below.
reason: The D-ratio puts technical dispersion (pooled QC) over the study samples' dispersion. A low D-ratio therefore means biological variance dominates, which marks a good feature. Broadhurst et al. 2018 set the acceptance criterion at 'at most, < 50% (preferably much lower)', so features above 50% are the ones removed. As written, the rule discards the features that carry the most biological signal and keeps the ones dominated by technical noise. Freezing the QC SD and taking the study SD per fold are defensible leakage controls, but they cannot rescue the reversed direction.

citations.cite: Broadhurst D et al. Guidelines and considerations for the use of system suitability and quality control samples in mass spectrometry assays applied in untargeted clinical metabolomic studies. Metabolomics 2018;14:72 (D-ratio acceptance < 50%)

bite_note: It decides which metabolomic features enter the analysis. As written, it removes the biologically informative features and keeps the noise-dominated ones, which changes every downstream result.

narrowest_regime: Any p >= 5 (for p <= 4 the formula gives q = 0 and nothing is selected), with the base lasso selecting exactly q variables per half, tau in (0.5, 1], under MB's exchangeability of noise-variable selection and their weak 'not worse than random guessing' condition.
reason: With tau = 0.6, 2*tau - 1 = 0.2, and q = floor(sqrt(0.2 p)) gives q^2 <= 0.2 p, so the bound q^2/((2*tau - 1)p) is <= 1 by arithmetic. Shah & Samworth (2013) show that complementary pairs stability selection (CPSS) recovers exactly this Meinshausen-Buhlmann bound on E|S_CPSS intersect N| under the exchangeability and random-guessing conditions, and that it holds for every B, so B = 50 (their recommended default) is covered. One wording slip: the claim names only exchangeability, but the bound also needs the weak 'not worse than random guessing' condition, which the lasso satisfies in practice. The control is on the expected number of false selections, under an exchangeability assumption that is strong and often violated.

citations.cite: Meinshausen N, Buhlmann P. Stability selection. JRSS B 2010;72:417-473, Theorem 1

Shah RD, Samworth RJ. Variable selection with error control: another look at stability selection. JRSS B 2013;75:55-80 (arXiv:1105.5578): MB bound recovered for CPSS under exchangeability and random guessing, valid for all B; B = 50 recommended

bite_note: B, tau and q set which predictors the stability step keeps, and the stated E[V] <= 1 is the error statement the researcher reports.

failing_part: "if the share of rows removed times the leavers' largest SMD on the adjustment set is below 0.003697, removing the screen ... moves the exposure's estimate by less than 0.1 of its 95% interval half-width"
narrowest_regime: Only very small exclusion shares, about 1% or less, where even pure sampling movement stays under 0.1 half-width with high probability, and only if the leavers do not misreport the exposure itself. The 0.003697 value has no general validity; it is an empirical cut from one fixture.
reason: Even if the leavers are a random subset, so that the SMD is close to 0, dropping a share s of rows moves the estimate by sampling alone with SD = SE*sqrt(s/(1-s)), which is about 0.17 half-widths at s = 0.10, at any n. Simulation (n = 40,000, 10% random leavers): 89% of runs fell under the 0.003697 product, and 52% of those still moved the estimate by at least 0.1 half-width. Energy screens target misreporters, whose exposure is itself mismeasured, and an SMD on the adjustment set cannot see that: with leavers under-reporting the exposure by 40%, 91% of runs passed the product test and 78% of those moved the estimate by at least 0.1 half-width (median 0.19). The precise cut, calibrated on 9 cases from one NHANES fixture with a single held-out prediction, carries invented precision, and the 0.2 'act on it' cut has no stated derivation.
bite_note: It tells the researcher 'Doesn't change your numbers here' and routes the screen to a supplement line, when removing the screen can move the exposure estimate materially. That decides whether a sensitivity analysis or a limitation is reported.

failing_part: "gives an approximately valid 95% interval and test ... Prediction; any task"
narrowest_regime: Learners of moderate stability and moderate p/n, comparing the expected (unconditional) difference in score at training size (K-1)n/K. There the corrected test is near nominal or conservative; for two similar, stable models it is markedly conservative.
reason: The formula and rK - 1 df match Nadeau & Bengio's corrected resampled t as Bouckaert & Frank apply it to r x K CV. The n2/n1 correlation term is a heuristic, though, not a derived bound, and no unbiased variance estimator for K-fold CV exists in general (Bengio & Grandvalet 2004), so validity depends on how stable the learner is. In my 10 x 5 simulations, null size ranged 0.031-0.068 (naive t: 0.56-0.62). For a non-null difference, coverage was 0.998 for two stable models and 0.94 at moderate instability, but fell to 0.90 with highly unstable fits (OLS with p/n1 of 0.5-0.7), the misses all on one side. So 'approximately valid' holds broadly but not for 'any task'. Labelling the pairwise intervals descriptive and leaving the selection to BBC-CV is coherent, since BBC-CV debiases the winner's estimate and does not certify the pairwise 'ahead' sentences.

citations.cite: Nadeau C, Bengio Y. Inference for the generalization error. Mach Learn 2003;52:239-281
Bouckaert RR, Frank E. Evaluating the replicability of significance tests for comparing learning algorithms. PAKDD 2004, LNCS 3056:3-12
Bengio Y, Grandvalet Y. No unbiased estimator of the variance of K-fold cross-validation. JMLR 2004;5:1089-1105
Tsamardinos I, Greasidou E, Borboudakis G. Bootstrapping the out-of-sample predictions for efficient and accurate cross-validation (BBC-CV). Mach Learn 2018;107:1895-1922

bite_note: It drives the 'not distinguishable' and 'X is ahead' sentences and the baseline verdict. Compared with the naive t (size about 0.56), it changes them substantially. Its own error regime, unstable small-n fits, produces some false 'ahead' calls, and stable near-ties are reported as 'not distinguishable' more often than nominal.

failing_part: "since the UL applies to total intake" and "only if the recalls include supplements"
narrowest_regime: Nutrients whose UL covers intake from all sources (for example calcium, iron, zinc, vitamin D, selenium, phosphorus). For these, a share computed from recalls without supplements understates the share at potential risk, and the label should be read as a lower bound.
reason: For several nutrients the IOM UL does not apply to total intake. Magnesium's UL covers supplemental or pharmacological magnesium only, folate's covers synthetic folic acid only, niacin's and vitamin E's cover synthetic or supplemental forms, and vitamin A's covers preformed vitamin A only. For these nutrients, comparing usual total intake (food plus supplements) with the UL mislabels the share, so adding supplements does not make it a share at risk; the right comparison uses the relevant form only. Even where the UL does cover all sources, a foods-only share is not meaningless: it is a lower bound. The IOM's own wording is 'potentially at risk', not 'at risk'.

citations.cite: Linus Pauling Institute, Folate: FNB UL applies to folic acid from supplements and fortification; no adverse effects from food folate
Wikipedia, Dietary Reference Intake: magnesium UL specific to dietary supplement form; food magnesium does not cause the problem
Institute of Medicine. DRI summary tables, UL footnotes: Mg from pharmacological agents only; niacin, vitamin E, folate apply to synthetic forms; vitamin A as preformed only
Institute of Medicine. Dietary Reference Intakes: Applications in Dietary Assessment. 2000 (proportion above UL = potentially at risk)

bite_note: It sets the label on the share above the UL. For magnesium, folate, niacin, vitamin E and vitamin A, labelling a total-intake share 'at risk' overstates excess risk even when supplements are included. For the other nutrients, a foods-only share gets refused a label it could carry as a lower bound.

failing_part: "is a status at sampling and is correctly analyzed as counted over one period for everyone ... without asking about follow-up"
narrowest_regime: The outcome really is a cross-sectional status at the time of sampling (prevalent condition, survey item, case/control label in an unmatched design), or an incident outcome with complete and equal follow-up for every participant.
reason: A missing column that reads as follow-up time is absence of evidence, not evidence that the outcome is a status at sampling. Metabolomic and genomic data are often assayed on baseline samples in prospective cohorts, with incident disease ascertained over follow-up that varies between people, and are often analysed in nested case-control or case-cohort designs. Follow-up may also be stored under an unrecognized name, or not supplied at all. In those settings a single-period binary model ignores unequal follow-up and censoring, and in matched nested designs it ignores the matching, which biases or changes the estimand. One question would separate the cases. Skipping it is safe only when the outcome is a cross-sectional status or follow-up is fixed and complete.
bite_note: For an incident outcome with variable follow-up or a matched nested design, it decides between a binary model and a time-to-event (or conditional) analysis, and so changes the estimate and its meaning.

failing_part: "the sound missing-data handling for inference is multiple imputation with the group in the imputation model" (stated without MI's own MAR and congeniality conditions)
narrowest_regime: Missingness is MAR given group and other observed variables, the imputation model includes the outcome, the group, and any group-by-variable interactions the analysis estimates, and either group is not in the analysis model or missingness is related to the outcome. There, MI with group is valid and complete-case analysis may be biased.
reason: Group-dependent missingness in predictors does not by itself bias complete-case regression. CCA stays unbiased for the coefficients whenever missingness is independent of the outcome given the model covariates, for example when group is itself an analysis covariate (White & Carlin 2010). In that case MI adds efficiency, not validity. MI is not assumption-free either: it needs MAR, and an imputation model that contains the outcome and is congenial with the analysis. Imputing with group only as a main effect biases group interactions toward zero, and when missingness depends on the missing value itself, MI is biased where CCA of Y on X need not be. The recommendation's direction is standard and the CCA caveat is correct, but calling MI 'the sound' handling while only CCA must state an assumption overstates the case.

citations.cite: White IR, Carlin JB. Bias and efficiency of multiple imputation compared with complete-case analysis for missing covariate values. Stat Med 2010;29:2920-2931
Sterne JAC et al. Multiple imputation for missing data in epidemiological and clinical research: potential and pitfalls. BMJ 2009;338:b2393
Moons KGM et al. Using the outcome for imputation of missing predictor values was preferred. J Clin Epidemiol 2006;59:1092-1101

bite_note: It decides between MI and CCA. When missingness relates to the outcome, or group is absent from the analysis model, the estimates differ. When group is already an analysis covariate and missingness does not depend on the outcome, the choice changes only precision.

narrowest_regime: Batch is a nominal label (plate, run, site code) adjusted as a fixed-effect covariate. With an intercept, 'one indicator per batch' means B - 1 indicators. For two batches, numeric 0/1 coding is already equivalent, so the confirmation is harmless but changes nothing.
reason: A batch label is nominal. Entering integer codes as one numeric covariate imposes a single linear trend across arbitrary labels, which removes neither the batch offsets nor the confounding they carry once there are three or more batches. Fixed-effect batch adjustment therefore needs one indicator per batch (B - 1 alongside an intercept). A numeric dtype cannot tell a batch code apart from a real quantity, such as run order meant to model drift, so asking for confirmation before accepting the column as a categorical covariate is the right guard. Random-effect or ComBat-type adjustments are alternatives, but they belong to other batch methods, not the 'covariate' method.
bite_note: With three or more batches coded as integers, the guard changes the adjustment from an arbitrary linear trend in the codes to proper per-batch offsets, which changes the adjusted estimates.

failing_part: "They therefore rank below the spline (and the straight line)"
narrowest_regime: A continuous exposure (not a confounder) whose dose-response is close to linear or smooth and monotone. There the quintile contrast is a legitimate, sample-defined between-group contrast with less power than continuous modelling, and ranking it below the spline and the line is justified.
reason: For an exposure, quintile coefficients do estimate real adjusted between-group contrasts. They are coarse and depend on the sample's cut-points (Bennette & Vickers 2012), but they are not false, and ranking them below a spline is well supported (Greenland 1995; Royston, Altman & Sauerbrei 2006). The 'therefore' over the straight line does not follow from the reasons given. Discarding within-fifth variation costs power, but the straight line makes its own shape assumption, and for U- or J-shaped responses, common in nutrition, a step function can describe the relation better than a misspecified linear slope. Placing the line above quintiles is a convention that holds under approximate linearity. The 'not a false number' framing also does not extend to quintiling a confounder, which leaves residual confounding.

citations.cite: Bennette C, Vickers A. Against quantiles: categorization of continuous variables in epidemiologic research, and its discontents. BMC Med Res Methodol 2012;12:21
Greenland S. Avoiding power loss associated with categorization and ordinal scores in dose-response and trend analysis. Epidemiology 1995;6:450-454
Royston P, Altman DG, Sauerbrei W. Dichotomizing continuous predictors in multiple regression: a bad idea. Stat Med 2006;25:127-141

Turner EL, Dobson JE, Pocock SJ. Categorisation of continuous risk factors in epidemiological publications: a survey of current practice. Epidemiol Perspect Innov 2010;7:9 (describes practice; does not endorse quintiles)

bite_note: It bites only once the researcher sets the spline aside. Then the line-over-quintiles order steers toward a straight line, which misstates a non-monotone dose-response. Not blocking quintiles changes nothing unless they are chosen.

failing_part: "is a sound model update that corrects for overfitting" (unconditionally, across the stated regime)
narrowest_regime: Pre-specified predictors, with the bootstrap repeating every modelling step, and an effective sample size that meets current development criteria (e.g., Riley et al. 2020) so the shrinkage factor is precisely estimated. There, uniform shrinkage with intercept re-estimation improves expected calibration, usually modestly.
reason: Uniform shrinkage by the bootstrap optimism-corrected slope, with the intercept refitted using the shrunk linear predictor as an offset, is the standard van Houwelingen & le Cessie / Steyerberg procedure, and it corrects overfitting on average. In a given dataset, though, the estimated shrinkage factor is itself very noisy exactly where overfitting is large. Riley et al. (2021) found bootstrap S ranging 0.43-1.21 at n = 50, and calibration slopes on validation still far from 1 after shrinkage, concluding these methods 'are more unreliable when needed most'. Where n is large enough for S to be precise, S is close to 1 and the update changes little. The out-of-fold CV slope comes from models trained on (K-1)/K of the data, so it slightly over-shrinks, and it misses selection steps that the resampling does not repeat.

citations.cite: Riley RD et al. Penalization and shrinkage methods produced unreliable clinical prediction models especially when sample size was small. J Clin Epidemiol 2021;132:88-96 (includes bootstrap and heuristic uniform shrinkage)
Van Calster B et al. Regression shrinkage methods for clinical prediction models do not guarantee improved performance: simulation study. Stat Methods Med Res 2020;29:3166-3178
Van Houwelingen JC, le Cessie S. Predictive value of statistical models. Stat Med 1990;9:1303-1325
Steyerberg EW. Clinical Prediction Models, 2nd ed. 2019, ch. 13

bite_note: It changes the deployed coefficients. In small samples, where S differs materially from 1, the shrunk model can be badly miscalibrated in either direction, so presenting the update as a sound fix may stand in for the real remedy, a larger sample or a penalized fit with its uncertainty reported.

narrowest_regime: Exact for linear-predictor models: the standard (N + E), residual (r + E), partition and substitution (all components but one, plus total) forms span the same column space and give identical fitted predictions. Approximate for the nutrient-density form (N/E + E), for penalized fits, and for tree ensembles.
reason: With total energy kept, the standard, residual, partition and substitution parameterizations are linear reparameterizations of one another, so unpenalized linear models predict identically and the choice only changes what a coefficient means. That is an estimation question in Shmueli's sense, and Willett's energy models answer it. Simulation (n = 2000, outcome driven by nutrient density): OLS CV R2 was 0.3488 for both standard and residual against 0.3550 for density; ridge gave the same pattern; gradient boosting gave 0.215 / 0.204 / 0.217. The nonlinear and density forms differ by about 0.01 R2. That fits 'predict alike' read as approximately, not identically. Entering nutrients as recorded beside total energy lets a flexible learner build any of these forms.

citations.cite: Willett WC, Howe GR, Kushi LH. Adjustment for total energy intake in epidemiologic studies. Am J Clin Nutr 1997;65(4 Suppl):1220S-1228S
Shmueli G. To explain or to predict? Stat Sci 2010;25:289-310

bite_note: Asking the energy-model question under Predict would change predictive performance by at most about 0.01 R2 in realistic settings, and not at all for linear models. Skipping it changes no prediction decision.
